sentences.text: Deinocheirus was the largest ornithomimosaur, reaching 11 meters in length and weighing 6.5 tons.
The only known skull measures 1.024 meters from the premaxilla to the occipital condyle.
It and Therizinosaurus possess the longest forelimbs of any known bipedal dinosaurs.
Its vertebrae featured an interconnected ligament system that stiffened the spine to support the abdomen while transferring stress to the hips and hind limbs.
Paleontologist Thomas R. Holtz described the skeleton as resembling a hybrid between a hadrosaur and Gallimimus.
The first remains were discovered in 1965 in the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia.
Polish paleontologist Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska found these initial remains on July 9, 1965.
Two new specimens were announced in 2013 at the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology conference.
Deinocheirus is thought to have been omnivorous, with evidence including fish scales found near a specimen and gastroliths in its stomach region.
The animal likely used its long arms and blunt claws for digging and gathering plants.
It had a weak bite force due to small muscle attachment sites relative to skull size.
Deinocheirids were not built for running, unlike other ornithomimosaurians.
Pygostyle-like vertebrae at the end of the tail indicate that Deinocheirus possessed a fan of feathers.
The tail ended in at least two fused vertebrae described as similar to the pygostyles of oviraptorosaurian and therizinosaurian theropods.
Researchers suspect Deinocheirus may have reverted to an omnivorous or carnivorous diet.
Deinocheirus is classified as a primitive ornithomimosaurian closely related to Garudimimus and Beishanlong, forming the family Deinocheiridae.
Osmólska and Roniewicz created the new family Deinocheiridae within Carnosauria because they believed Deinocheirus did not fit existing theropod families.
A 2014 cladogram suggested ornithomimosaurians split into Deinocheiridae and Ornithomimidae lineages in the Early Cretaceous.
Deinocheirids and smaller ornithomimids lacked teeth, unlike more primitive ornithomimosaurs.
Deinocheirus lived during the Late Cretaceous approximately 70 million years ago.
Deinocheirus mirificus lived between 71 and 69 million years ago during the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Asia.
The river habitats where Deinocheirus lived supported a wide variety of other organisms including fish, turtles, and birds.
Researchers tested geochemical methods to identify poached Deinocheirus fossils because proving provenance became a scientific and political concern.
Researchers suggest deinocheirids either originated in Laurasia or dispersed across Northern Hemisphere polar regions, similar to other Asian-affinity dinosaur groups.
The function of pneumatization in Deinocheirus is debated, with hypotheses including bone mass reduction, high metabolism, locomotion balance, or thermoregulation.
